done.why: I had just typed 'go east' to try the crack by the chasm when the world told me I had used all 30 turns. I was about ready to quit anyway: after the troll it was corridor after corridor with dead ends and nothing to pick up or do.

about: The Zork opening — mailbox, white house, kitchen, lantern and sword, trap door — but once you're underground and past the troll, the familiar map has collapsed. Passages are choked with cave-ins, someone has been tidying the rubble into neat sorted heaps, and the chasm path drowns in cold black water. It feels like a version of the dungeon that has been abandoned and is slowly falling in on itself, with some unseen tidy person still living in it.

moments.note: The leaflet's 'No computer should be without one!' — I grinned.
The trap door crashing shut and someone barring it behind me. Who?
Missed the troll and got knocked to my knees on the first swing.
Took the troll's head on the fourth swing; the black fog eating the body was a nice touch.
The Round Room is caved in — this is where the place stops being the one I half expected.
Somebody sorted the rubble into heaps, smallest nearest, 'the way some people tidy a room they have no intention of using.' Best line in the game.
'examine heaps' gave the exact same paragraph as 'examine cave-ins'. Wanted more.
South was a dead end, repeated the same description a third time.
The chasm path runs down into black still water with no far side — the game walked me back with wet feet. Atmospheric.
'enter crack' not understood, and then the turn cap hit before I could try 'east'.

wished: Dig at or climb the rubble heaps, or move the sorted rocks — the game drew my eye to them and then gave me nothing to do with them.
Find out who barred the trap door and who is sorting rocks; some trace of that person.
Go through the crack by the chasm with a plain verb like 'enter crack'.
Have the examine text vary when I looked closer at the heaps, instead of repeating the room description.

lines.line: The trap door crashes shut, and you hear someone barring it.
lines.why: First sign that there's somebody else down here, and that I can't go back.

lines.line: It's curtains for the troll as your sword removes his head.
lines.why: The one real payoff of the session — a fight I could lose, won.

lines.line: somebody has sorted the nearest of it into neat heaps, smallest nearest, the way some people tidy a room they have no intention of using.
lines.why: The only line that made me curious about the changed world — it implies a person with habits, and I wanted to meet them.

lines.line: the path runs down into water, black and still and very cold, and your light finds no other side to it. You go back the way you came, with wet feet.
lines.why: Good dead-end writing; it felt like a place rather than a wall.

fun.why: The troll fight and the collapsed Round Room were good, but after that it was dead ends and a parser miss, and I ran out of turns before anything new happened.

engagement.why: The barred trap door and the tidy rock-sorter hooked me, but three rooms in a row with nothing to interact with let it slip.

difficulty.why: Nothing was hard; the only challenge was the troll, which was just repeated swinging. The rest was finding which corridor wasn't blocked.

interestingness.why: The idea of the old dungeon caving in and flooding, with someone still tidying it, is a genuinely interesting change and the descriptions sold it.

prose.why: The new writing (heaps, black water) is sharp and specific; the repetition of the same cave-in paragraph three times dragged it down.
